note: Editorial vocabulary. Aliases are search conveniences; they do not claim that two terms mean the same thing. Links are labelled 'same' (one idea, two names in the site's data) or 'near' (closely related, not identical).

concepts.label: Accountability
concepts.description: Accountability asks who answers for decisions in which AI systems take part. The archive records responsibility and the evaluation of awareness claims as unsettled questions.

concepts.label: Artificial Intelligence
concepts.description: Artificial intelligence studies and builds systems that perform tasks associated with learning, inference, perception, and language. Its connection to human experience raises questions about knowledge, agency, and understanding.

concepts.label: Archives
concepts.description: Archives preserve selected traces of the past. Digital archives complicate who records, organizes, remembers, and interprets the lives represented in those traces.

concepts.label: Attention
concepts.description: Attention selects some information for further processing. The archive asks how attention and consciousness are related, and whether one can occur without the other.
concepts.tcDescription: Selective use of limited processing resources.

concepts.label: Awareness
concepts.tcDescription: Being aware of a stimulus or mental state, as the term is used by the theories here.

concepts.label: Cognition
concepts.description: Cognition includes attention, reasoning, learning, and information processing. Studying human cognition offers useful comparisons with AI while also revealing important differences.

concepts.label: Computing History
concepts.description: The history of computing is where the question 'Can machines think?' was first posed formally. Turing's imitation game and Searle's reply anchor the scholarly timeline kept in the archive.

concepts.label: Consciousness
concepts.description: Consciousness names the subjective dimension of experience: what it is like to perceive, think, and be aware. Whether and how this could relate to machine systems remains an open philosophical and scientific question.

concepts.label: Digital Culture
concepts.description: Digital culture describes how technologies, platforms, and shared practices shape expression, memory, creativity, and collective life.

concepts.label: Digital Minds
concepts.description: Digital minds gathers questions about digital representations of people and about artificial memory and self-representation. What such systems preserve of a person is left open.

concepts.label: Emergence
concepts.description: Emergence asks whether consciousness is a fundamental feature of reality or arises from physical processes. The theories compared in the Theory Chamber take different positions.

concepts.label: Ethics & Society
concepts.description: Ethics and society ask what we owe to, and how we should hold accountable, increasingly capable artificial systems. The archive treats moral consideration and responsibility as open questions.

concepts.label: Global availability
concepts.tcDescription: Making a representation available to many specialized processors at once.

concepts.label: Identity
concepts.description: Identity concerns the narratives, relationships, records, and experiences through which a person becomes recognizable to themselves and others, including through digital traces.

concepts.label: Information processing
concepts.tcDescription: How a system takes in, transforms, and uses information.

concepts.label: Integration
concepts.tcDescription: Unity of information within a system, as the term is used in IIT.

concepts.label: Intelligence
concepts.description: Intelligence is the capacity to solve problems, reason, and adapt. The archive asks whether it can be separated from consciousness and from self-awareness.

concepts.label: Language
concepts.description: Language makes meanings shareable, yet fluent language alone does not establish understanding or awareness. It forms a bridge and a boundary between human communication and machine output.

concepts.label: Machine Learning
concepts.description: Machine learning builds systems that improve at tasks from data. Here it is discussed in relation to what such systems do and do not show about understanding, memory, and mind.

concepts.label: Machine consciousness
concepts.tcDescription: Whether artificial systems could be conscious.

concepts.label: Memory
concepts.description: Memory preserves and reconstructs information across time. Comparing human remembering with computational storage raises questions about continuity, interpretation, and the limits of machine analogy.

concepts.label: Metacognition
concepts.tcDescription: Thinking about one's own mental states.

concepts.label: Evidence & Method
concepts.description: Method is how claims about the mind get tested. Adversarial collaboration, evidence classification, and honest 'awaiting review' labels run through this site's research tools.

concepts.label: Philosophy of Mind
concepts.description: Philosophy of mind asks what minds are and how they relate to bodies and brains. Its questions about subjective experience and mental states frame much of what the scientific theories try to explain.

concepts.label: Moral Status
concepts.description: Moral status concerns which beings an agent has duties toward. The archive treats the conditions under which an artificial system could deserve moral consideration as an open question.

concepts.label: Neural activity
concepts.tcDescription: Brain activity that can be recorded and compared across conscious and nonconscious conditions.

concepts.label: Neuroscience
concepts.description: Neuroscience studies the nervous system. On this site it is the home of questions about which neural processes accompany conscious experience, and of the competing theories that try to say.

concepts.label: Perception
concepts.description: Perception is how organisms take in and interpret the world. Questions here include how conscious perception differs from unconscious processing, which is a test case for theories of consciousness.

concepts.label: Prediction
concepts.tcDescription: Generation and updating of predictions about incoming signals.

concepts.label: Reasoning
concepts.description: Reasoning is the drawing of conclusions from information. The archive asks whether machine reasoning can become functionally comparable to human reasoning, and what such a comparison would show.

concepts.label: Recurrent processing
concepts.tcDescription: Feedback activity within and between processing stages.

concepts.label: Self & Selfhood
concepts.description: The self is the sense of being one continuous someone. Here it covers how the brain might construct that sense, how it relates to self-awareness, and whether an AI system could represent itself.

concepts.label: Self-modeling
concepts.tcDescription: A system's internal model of itself or of its own processes.

concepts.label: Subjective experience
concepts.tcDescription: What it is like, from the inside, to perceive, think, and feel.

concepts.label: Meaning & Understanding
concepts.description: Understanding asks whether grasping meaning differs from producing fitting outputs. Turing's imitation game and Searle's argument frame the debate, and the question remains contested.
